◇ There is no flaw. That is what you keep failing to hear. He was not wrong about anything. Every step of his reasoning was sound.
◦ Then soundness killed him. You would have me admire that.

◇ I would have you see it. A man followed the truth further than the truth can be followed and stayed alive, and the truth did not stop being the truth at the point where it began to cost him. You want a flaw so you can believe it will not come for you.

Nothing answers.
I want to tell you about the ones who stayed. Because a sealed centre is not only something that happens to the one inside it. It happens, differently, to everyone who loved him.

There was a woman who cooked for me. I will not say more about her than that, because more is not mine to give, but she cooked, and she brought it, and she watched me not eat it, and here is what I need you to understand about what that did.

She could see that the food was safe. Of course she could. It was safe. She had made it safe with her own hands, and she carried the proof of its safety in every ordinary certainty a person walks around inside, the certainty I had lost. So to her there was no problem. There was only a man refusing a solved problem. And you cannot stand outside a sealed centre and see why it will not open, because from the outside the centre looks exactly like a choice.

That is the cruelty of it, running the other way. Inside, I was not choosing. Outside, all she could see was choice. The same act, the refusal of the fork, was to me a wall I could not pass and to her a decision I would not make, and no words I had could carry her across the distance between those two readings, because the distance was the wall itself, and the wall does not let meaning through in either direction.
She measured me. That is what the ones outside are left to do.

She learned the exact weight I would lose in a week. The point at which the doctors would say a word. The numbers, the distances, the hour of the last time I had eaten anything at all. She became an investigator on the slope of me.

She built her Afterfact around a centre that gave her nothing back. Every fact she gathered was correct, and not one of them was the answer she needed, which was only to reach me. I was sealed. She could not.

I watched her do it. That is the part I cannot set down. I watched her circle me the way the careful circle any closed object, certain that one more meal offered differently, one more word, one more angle of approach would be the one that opened the door, and there was no door, and I could not tell her there was no door, because telling her would have required her to believe a thing that from her side was indistinguishable from my simply refusing to try.
So she stayed on the rim of me and called it love, and it was love, and it did not reach, and both of those are true.
There is a question you are wanting to ask by now, and you are being too polite, so I will ask it for you.
Why did I not simply choose to live?

You want there to have been a door I would not open. It is a kinder world if the door was there and I refused it, because then the fault is mine and the wall is not real and you are safe, because you would have opened it. I understand the wish. I had it about other people, before it was my turn.
But listen, because this is the centre around which everything else has been arranged.

The ability to stop was not a power I had and withheld. It was a thing I had lost, the way you can lose the ability to fall asleep by watching yourself try. Sleep will not come to the one who observes his own falling. And certainty will not close for the one who has learned to watch the closing, because the closing was never a reasoned act. It happened below reason, and once you have dragged it up into the light and looked at it, you cannot put it back down into the dark where it worked.
I looked at the mechanism that lets a person stop asking. That was my whole life's work, to look at it.

And a man who has truly seen the mechanism by which belief closes can no longer let his own belief close. For the same reason a man who has seen the wires cannot watch the magic. The trick requires that you not see the wires.
I saw the wires. I could not un-see them to save my own life, and I mean that with no metaphor at all.
Now turn it toward yourself, because I did not tell you any of this so that you could pity a dead logician.

You stop pulling the thread a hundred times a day. You have already done it several times while reading this. Something in these pages opened a small gap under one of your certainties, and you felt the first thread come up, and you set it down and kept reading, and you did not notice you had decided to. That setting-down is what I lost. It is doing its quiet work in you right now, and you cannot see it, and its invisibility is exactly the proof that it is working.

You call it common sense. You call it being reasonable, being grounded, having your feet on the ground. But name the ground. Go on. Name the ground your feet are on, and then name what that is on, and follow it the way I followed it, and tell me where you stop and why.

You will stop. That is my whole point, and it is not an accusation, it is almost a blessing. You will stop, and you will not be able to fully justify where, and you will walk across the floor anyway, and the floor will hold, and you will have done what I could not do, which is to trust a ground you cannot prove.

I could not, and it killed me. You can, and it saves your life every single day, and you have never once thanked it, because you have never once seen it, because seeing it is the beginning of not being able to do it.

So here is the thing I message out of the sealed centre, the one message the closure let me send before it shut. Do not learn to see the wires. It sounds like the opposite of wisdom. Every instinct this book has trained in you says look closer, follow it down, do not be fooled. And I am telling you, from the inside of what that costs, that the ability to stop looking is not a weakness in your thinking. It is the floor your thinking stands on, and if you ever fully succeed in analysing it, you will find yourself, as I found myself, standing on nothing, in a full and edgeless nothing, at a table laid with food you can no longer lift.
They found me at the end weighing almost nothing, which is the detail everyone remembers, and it is the wrong detail, though I understand why you keep it in the back of your mind.

They remember the weight because the weight is a number, and a number is something you can hold, and holding it lets you stand near the sealed centre of me without falling in. The weight is furniture. It is the safest fact in the whole account, and so it is the one that survives, and the survival of the safe fact over the true one is the last lesson my life has to teach, and I would rather you learned it from the number than not at all.
But the truth was not the weight.

It was that I reached the place this book has been walking toward from its first page, and I reached it not by crossing anything but by being closed, and what I can tell you about that place, having been sealed inside it, is the one report no one else in these pages can give, because the others all stand outside the wall and I was the wall.

It is not empty in there. That is the whole of what I have to say, and I have said it before, and I will say it once more because it is the error the living most need to keep making. You imagine the far side of the wall as blankness, as nothing, as the absence at the end of everything. It is not absence. It is presence with no way to move through it. It is everything you ever knew, arrived all at once, standing around you at an even and unbearable pressure, complete, seamless, and closed. A plenum, not a void. The terror was never that nothing was there. The terror was that everything was, and that I could no longer take it one step at a time.

And I could not send that back. Not really. The notes went out calm and legible and evenly spaced, and none of them carried the thing itself, because the thing itself was sealed behind them, the way the reason was sealed behind the footprints, the way the beginning is always sealed behind the field it pays out.
You are reading the footprints now.

They are calm, and evenly spaced, and they came down out of a place you cannot follow them back into, and you are standing at the topmost print looking up at clean snow, and there is no next mark, and there is no reason given, and the record is complete, and the record is not the thing.
The thing does not come down the mountain. It never has. It stays where it closed, full and edgeless and silent, and lets the world have everything about it except itself.

I stayed there. I am there in whatever way a sealed centre is anywhere. And the last mercy left to me, the only one the closure did not take, is that you are not there, that your questions still shut, that your floor still holds, that you can put this book down and eat something and not know why you are able to, and be saved, exactly, by the not-knowing.
Do not follow me up the mountain. There is nothing at the top but the view of how far down everything is.

▪ I meant it before he showed me what it was. Stopping. He made stopping sound like the thing a smaller man does, and I am the one who stops, and now I do not know if I am well or only shallow.

CHAPTER VI · THE TRAJECTORY
The end announces itself early, to some people, in the middle of the beginning.
Everyone knows the low fear that a good thing will stop. It sits under a happy year and means little. What arrives around the third month, lying beside her in the dark, is not that hum at all.

It is a trajectory, cold and complete. You can see the exact shape of the failure, the fault that will open it, the season it opens in, even the sentence one of you will say that the other cannot forgive. Her hand is warm on your chest. She is saying the things people say when they believe nothing between them is about to give way. And the whole curve of its collapse is already legible to you, from inside its first inch.

Foresight was supposed to be a gift. Everyone who has ever wished for it imagined the same reward, which was to see the crash coming and turn the wheel in time. To see early is to steer. That was always the promise.
The wheel is not connected to the road.

You watch the bend approach for miles and your turning alters nothing, because the turn was plotted too. It sits on the same curve you are trying to escape, one more charted point, anticipated, folded into the very line it meant to break. She asks what you are thinking. You say nothing, though even your silence is on the graph.
What you see has the hard edges of a circuit diagram.

She needs to be chosen again and again, out loud, in a way she has never named and might not recognize in herself. You choose once, all the way down, and then treat the matter as closed and turn to other work. Two ordinary facts, and neither one ends a marriage in a week.
Together they end it in fourteen months. You can nearly mark the date, because arithmetic does not pause for the people currently inside the sum.

The steadiness she loves in you now is the same steadiness she will later call coldness. One trait, read as warmth at the start and read as rejection at the end. Nothing about it will have changed except her reading. That reading is hers. You get no hand in it.
The cruellest line on the whole graph is the effort still to come.

Counselling, the weekends booked to repair things, the long tender talks across a kitchen table, all of it real and all of it sincere and all of it already drawn. The trying is a marked segment of the descent. It was never outside the machine, only one of the motions the machine performs on its way down. Knowing this will not excuse you from performing it anyway, on schedule, with your whole heart.
The first move most people make is to distrust the vision, and the distrust is reasonable.

You tell yourself it is only morbidity in the costume of clarity, that nobody truly knows the future, that you are borrowing tomorrow's grief to ruin tonight. The snare is that half of it is true. Sometimes it really is only dread.

But a person who has run enough of these can feel the seam between the fear of a fall and the measurement of one. It is the same seam a mathematician feels between a hunch and a proof. Dread flutters. What you are holding does not flutter. It comes out even, every time.
The knowing that ruins a person is never the loud kind. Its whole horror is that it stays calm, because it is sure.

Once honest doubt is gone, you have arrived somewhere the earlier pages never went. The man on the slope did not know why he walked into the cold. The one who starved could not see into his own centre. Both of them were blind, sealed away from a truth they could not enter.

Your position reverses theirs, and the reversal is no kinder. Nothing is hidden from you. The interior of the future has been handed over whole, lit from within, every corner of it labelled and clear.
You are forbidden only to touch it.
The good days suffer the most, which is the part nobody warns you about. Foresight does not leave them alone. It ruins them with a special care.
She laughs on a Sunday at something small. The laugh is real, the light on the counter is real, the whole ordinary morning belongs to the two of you.

Over it lies the other Sunday, half-transparent, the one fourteen months out, when the same room will hold two people being gentle with each other and saying very little. You cannot lift the second morning off the first. The present loses its right to be only itself. Every hour you are handed comes with its ending already folded inside, the two delivered together, the joy and the date of the joy's death arriving in a single package.

Behind us sat a consequence with its cause sealed away, past all reaching. In front of you sits the same shape turned around, a consequence shown in advance, with the present sealed against your reaching it.

The graph pays out forward now instead of backward. You stand in your own present the way the searchers stood on the snow, holding a full and faultless account and bending none of it, because a map of the wreck was never a hand on the wheel.
All of it is yours. Every point on the curve. Everything except the one use you wanted the knowing for, which was to change where the curve arrives.
So the mind, being a mind, looks for the exit. There are only a few, and the vision has already followed each one to its end.

The first is to leave now, early, before the descent. End it in the third month while it is still good. Simply rob the curve of its fourteen months. Refuse the crash by refusing the drive. It feels, for an afternoon, like the one free act available, the single move the graph did not anticipate.
It did.

Leaving early is not an escape from the trajectory. It is the trajectory, arriving ahead of schedule by a different road. You will have produced the ending you foresaw, in the name of avoiding it, and the ending will not care which door it came through. The grief is the same grief. You merely paid it sooner and called the payment “freedom”.
The second exit runs the other way. Stay, refuse to look. Bury the calculation, throw yourself into the warm present, love her as though the graph were never drawn. Choose ignorance on purpose.

But a thing seen cannot be unseen by deciding to. You already know the mechanism a man uses to stop looking, and knowing it is exactly what keeps you from being able to use it. The one who has watched belief close can no longer let his own belief close. So the refusal to look becomes one more thing you are watching yourself do, narrated, transparent, and the second Sunday shows through the first no matter how hard you fix your eyes on the counter and the light.

The third exit is the quietest of the three. It is also the most tempting, though it is barely an exit at all. Tell her. Lay the whole graph on the kitchen table between you and let her see what you see. Surely two people, warned, can steer where one cannot.
They cannot. The warning is only more of the curve.

She will hear the warning through her own reading, the reading that is hers and not yours to set, and to her the man describing the inevitable death of the relationship is not a prophet doing her a kindness. He is a man withdrawing. He is the fourteen-month coldness, arriving early, wearing the mask of honesty. Your foresight, spoken aloud, one more step in the trajectory.
Every exit is a corridor drawn on the same map, leading back onto the road it promised to leave.
Step into one of the good mornings, all the way in, because the argument has been standing outside them and the standing outside is a kind of lie.

It is a Saturday. She is at the counter cutting fruit, still in the shirt she sleeps in, and the light comes in low and lays itself along her arm. She is telling you something about her sister. Watching the knife, the fruit, the light… you love her, and none of that is in question.

Laid over the whole scene, at the same depth, in the same focus, is the knowledge of the morning in the second autumn when she will stand at this same counter and not tell you about her sister, when the not-telling will be the whole language of the room.
Both mornings occupy you at once.

Not remembering one while living the other. Both, now, at the same instant, as two transparencies laid together make a third image belonging to neither. The Saturday is real. The second autumn is real. They occupy the same space in you, and you cannot make them stop. So the fruit, the light, the sister all arrive already carrying their own erasure. You smile at her. The smile is true. Behind it you are attending a funeral for a woman standing in front of you very much alive.
She sees the smile. She does not see the funeral. How could she?
Something worse than sadness grows out of this, and it takes a while to notice, because it wears the face of care.

The grieving for her begins in advance. Not by decision. It simply starts. Some evening she falls asleep against you on the couch, and instead of being there, in the warmth, with the weight of her head on your arm, you are already remembering this, from the far side of the ending, as a thing you used to have. The loss of the moment registers while the moment is still happening. A nostalgia for a present that has not yet left.
This is the second theft, larger than the first.

The first theft was the ending. The Given showed you the ending and that was cruel, but an ending is only one day, far off. The second theft is every day between now and then. Because a man pre-grieving cannot be in the room. He has moved his residence to the aftermath and only visits the present. The visits get shorter. She can feel him leaving without being able to name what he leaves toward, since the loss he is leaving toward has not occurred.

The whole aim was to protect the fourteen months. Instead the foreknowledge is eating them from inside, one evening at a time, so that the very thing you were trying to keep is being spent in mourning it. The graph did not have to wait fourteen months to take her from you. It took her the night you first saw the curve. Everything after is you, holding a woman who is present, and missing her.
There is a distance in the bed that has nothing to do with space.

She lies beside you living forward. For her the story runs the ordinary direction, one blind day handing to the next, the future a fog she leans into trusting there is ground. She does not know the ending. She gets to not know it. That not-knowing is what lets her rest her whole weight on the days, spend them without counting, be foolish and open and unguarded in a way that requires the future to stay dark.

You lie beside her living backward. You start from the ending and read toward now, and every day is not a step into fog but a step down a slope whose bottom you have already seen. You cannot be unguarded. Being unguarded requires not knowing where the road ends, and you know.

So the two of you are in the same bed on different clocks, moving through the same nights in opposite directions, passing each other. She reaches forward into a dark that is kind because it is dark. You reach backward into a light that is unkind because it is light. And you cannot join her in her direction. You cannot un-know the end and lean into the fog beside her. The most intimate thing, to share a time, to be inside the same unspooling hour together, is the one thing the Given has made impossible, because she has a future and you have only a foreseen past.
One could tell her the ending, to share a single clock. But that road has already been walked. So you keep the two clocks. You love her across the gap between them, and the gap does not close.
A temptation arrives, around here, disguised as rigor.

The testing begins. Nothing dramatic… only a watching for confirmations, the small proofs that the graph makes true. A comment she makes about needing more from you, and there it is, the first tremor of the fault you predicted, exactly on schedule. A Sunday she seems a little distant, and you file it, evidence, the curve holding true.
And the testing feels responsible. It feels like keeping honest track. Nothing is more natural than checking a prediction against the data coming in.
But watch what the checking does.

Every ambiguous moment, and most moments are ambiguous, you now read through the graph. The graph tells you which reading is true. Her quiet becomes withdrawal instead of tiredness. Your own reticence becomes the predicted coldness instead of an ordinary bad day. This is no longer a mere observation. It is scoring, the relationship measured against a prophecy; and the scoring selects, from every day, exactly the evidence that fits, discarding the rest without noticing.

So the prophecy starts to come true faster. Not because it was right, though it may have been. A man watching for an ending finds its beginnings everywhere. He treats her ordinary human weather as the confirmed approach of the storm; he responds to the confirmation, pulls back a little, guards a little more. She feels the pulling back and answers it. The curve you were only meant to watch has quietly taken your hands and begun to steer with them.

The Given does not only show you the road. It recruits you, without your consent, into building it. The prediction and the fulfilment stop being two things. The seer becomes the instrument by which the foreseen turns into the arranged, and there is no telling, from inside it, how much of the ending was seen and how much was caused, because from the driver's seat the wheel that does nothing and the wheel that does everything feel exactly the same in the hands.
Notice what has been assumed all along, under every exit? That the point of seeing the curve is to change it?

Strip that away and look at what remains. Because there is a version of the person who stops looking for a door, not out of despair, but because the search itself was the last unexamined superstition. You have been treating the vision as a problem to solve. What if it is simply a condition to inhabit?

The curve was handed to you. You did not ask for it and cannot return it. It was placed in your sight, whole, the day you understood her needs and your own and felt the two of them lock into their fourteen-month arithmetic. Placed there, without your consent, without your permission, and without the one accompanying gift that would have made it bearable, which is the power to act on it.
This is what a person is finally left holding. A given.
So she asks, again, on some ordinary night, what you are thinking.

And this time, understanding everything, seeing the whole graph lit and labelled and running toward its close, holding the given in both hands like a stone you cannot set down, you stay. You do not leave in the third month to cheat the curve. You do not blind yourself to love her more easily. You do not lay the diagram on the table and call it honesty.
You stay, and you love her, and you drive the curve you can see the end of.

Not because you have found the exit. There is none. Because the alternative to driving a doomed road is to never have driven with her at all. That alternative is worse than the crash. The arithmetic that condemns the relationship holds no term for it, no variable for the worth of the fourteen months themselves, which were never the wreckage on the way to an ending. They were the thing itself. The only thing. The whole of what there was to have.
The graph does not know this. The graph measures descent and cannot see that the descent was worth taking.
◦ Why choose to suffer? He saw the wall coming and drove at it on purpose. Name the sense in that.
◇ He chose the fourteen months. The wall was never the choice. The wall was only the price of the months, and he read the price and paid it and did not pretend the price was smaller than it was.
◦ The price was everything. It ended. All of it ended.

◇ Everything ends. He knew the ending more precisely than any of us and loved her anyway, and you cannot find the flaw in it, so you call it suffering, because suffering is a category you know how to stand next to.
▪ I would not have driven. I would have seen the curve and stepped out of the car.
◇ And kept nothing. And been safe. You keep choosing the empty room over the doomed one because the empty room cannot hurt you, and you call the choosing wisdom.
▪ It is not wisdom. I know that now. It is only the thing I can survive.

◇ He drove because the months were worth the wall. You would not, because you cannot yet stand inside a thing that ends. Neither position is a proof. They are two ways of holding the same given, and nothing measured so far can weigh one against the other.
Nothing answers.
